conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, which simply means I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers. First, congratulations on your baby; the postpartum weeks can feel like riding a roller-coaster, and it’s completely normal to need a little extra support.

Today I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to check in on how you’ve been feeling. This is a short, 10-question screening that looks at mood, anxiety, and thoughts you may have had over the past seven days. It isn’t a test you can pass or fail; it’s just a snapshot to help us understand what kind of support would be most helpful for you right now.

Everything you share stays confidential within your care team, and there’s no judgment here—only curiosity and care. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer in whatever words feel comfortable for you. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.

Let’s start: Looking back over the past week, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you used to, or has that felt different for you lately?

I guess… it’s just felt different. Like, I used to love making dinner with my husband—music on, glass of wine, talking about anything. Now I make the same meal and it feels like one more chore. Even when the baby’s asleep and I have a free hour, I scroll my phone or fold laundry instead of picking up my knitting or texting friends. Nothing sounds appealing, really.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly the same as before… every once in a while I’ll chuckle at something, but it feels forced, like I’m reminding myself “this is supposed to be funny.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I keep thinking I should look forward to little outings—like taking the baby for a walk or grabbing coffee—but when the time comes, I just feel tired and kind of “what’s the point?” Yesterday my sister texted about meeting at the park, and instead of feeling excited I felt this wave of dread about getting us both ready.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. Last night the baby was fussy for almost an hour and I kept thinking it must be something I ate, or maybe I’m not holding him right. When he finally settled, instead of feeling relieved I just sat there crying, telling my husband it was my fault for not figuring it out sooner. Even little stuff—like forgetting to bring a burp cloth to the couch—makes me feel like I’m failing at being his mom.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly worry his breathing sounds different, so I’m staring at his chest instead of resting. Or I’ll lie down and think, “What if the crib rail isn’t locked right?”—and I have to get up to check, even if I already checked an hour ago. I know it’s probably fine, but the thoughts just race until I do something to calm them.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a sudden rush—my heart starts racing and I feel shaky, like something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s going on. The other night I was just rocking the baby in the dark and out of nowhere I felt like I couldn’t breathe, like the walls were closing in. It passed after a minute, but it left me rattled.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most of the time. It’s like the second I finish one thing—feeding, changing, pumping—there’s already another bottle to wash or laundry pile staring at me. I’ll sit down to rest and hear the baby stir, and this wave of “I can’t keep up” just hits. I manage to do the basics, but it feels like I’m barely treading water every single day.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

A few nights this week. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—going over everything I might have messed up or worrying about the next feed. I’ll finally drift off, then the tiniest whimper from the bassinet jolts me awake and I can’t settle again for an hour or more.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a weight on my chest. I’ll watch the baby smile and think, “I should be happy right now,” but this cloud just hangs there. Some mornings I cry while brushing my teeth because everything feels so gray before the day’s even started.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… a few times this week. Yesterday I spilled a half-pumped bottle of milk on the counter and just stood there sobbing—couldn’t stop. It wasn’t about the milk; it felt like everything was crashing down in that moment.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I’m exhausted and overwhelmed, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby needs.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item self-report, clinician-reviewed

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, sadness (“weight on chest,” morning tearfulness)  
- Marked anhedonia (loss of anticipatory joy; “what’s the point?”)  
- Daily tearfulness / crying spells, often precipitated by minor stressors  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding parenting performance (“failing as his mom”)  
- Psychic & somatic anxiety: racing thoughts, intrusive worries about infant safety, nocturnal checking, episodic panic symptoms (palpitations, dyspnea)  
- Sleep disturbance secondary to ruminations and hypervigilance toward infant  
- Global sense of being overwhelmed, “treading water,” difficulty coping with routine infant care  

Pattern  
Symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, beginning post-delivery; no periods of euthymia reported; functional impairment in self-care and infant care tasks.

Screening significance  
High endorsement for items consistent with major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety. No self-harm ideation reported (Q10 denied). No current safety concerns identified.

Risk factors identified  
- Primiparous status, sleep deprivation, high self-expectations  
- Absence of protective mood buffers (loss of pleasure, social withdrawal)  
- Anxiety-driven maternal behaviors (repetitive checking, safety rituals)

Summary  
Patient screens positive for moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; self-harm risk currently denied. Recommend expedited follow-up with OB/midwife and referral for comprehensive perinatal mental health evaluation to confirm diagnosis and initiate appropriate level of care.
